summary.workload_description: Evaluated 5000 normalized 768-dimensional float vectors (3800 target namespace 'test_iter_target_ns', 1200 background namespace 'test_iter_distractor_ns'). The target namespace contains 76% of the dataset, so the workload is not globally highly selective by table partition. However, the distractor namespace contains 50 background vectors specifically perturbed to be much closer to the query vector (cosine distance ~0.0002–0.0012) than any target namespace vector (cosine distance ~0.0112). This creates a challenging post-filtering scenario.
summary.recall_conclusion: Iterative scanning ('strict_order' and 'relaxed_order') demonstrated a decisive recall improvement over default retrieval ('off'). Across all tested ef_search values (10, 40, 100, 200), default retrieval returned 0 candidates (0.0 Recall@5, 0.0 Recall@10) because the ef_search candidate budget was exhausted entirely on closer background distractor vectors that were pruned by the namespace filter. Iterative scanning continued graph traversal past filtered distractor vectors to retrieve all 10 target candidates, achieving full recall (1.0 Recall@1, 1.0 Recall@5, 1.0 Recall@10, 10/10 exact top-K overlap) across all tested configurations. Diagnostic EXPLAIN ANALYZE row counts matched measured retrieval counts exactly across all configurations (0 rows for 'off', 10 rows for iterative modes).
summary.latency_conclusion: Latency measurements reflect the algorithmic trade-off: default retrieval ('off') terminates quickly after examining ef_search candidates without joining cache entries (since 0 candidates survive filtering), while iterative scanning ('strict_order' and 'relaxed_order') incurs additional graph traversal and 10 cache index lookups to find valid matching entries. Iterative scanning improves candidate completeness under post-filtering by continuing HNSW traversal, subject to configured scan limits; it is not a latency reduction optimization.
